text: Johnson's praise of Shakespeare rests upon one principle, which he lays down without ornament: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature." (Johnson 1765). The dramatists who wrote beside Shakespeare had, in his account, drawn men as the customs of some particular court or city had formed them. Their figures were cut to the fashion of a season; they spoke the cant of a coterie, and turned upon the follies of a single year. Such figures could not outlast the occasion that produced them. When the fashion changed their force was spent, and a later reader finds in them nothing but the dress of a time that has gone. Shakespeare's persons, Johnson holds, are of another make. They act and speak by those passions and principles which are common to every age and every country; a father's grief or a counsellor's vanity is the same in Elsinore as in London, and the same now as when the plays were first acted. Johnson does not deny that the plays bear the marks of their own day. He holds only that these marks lie upon the surface, and that beneath them stands the common nature of mankind. It is because of this common nature that a reader who knows nothing of Elizabethan manners can still believe in Polonius.
